questionText:
Choose the correct statements about the Virupaksha temple at Hampi:
 
(A) The hall in front of the main shrine was built by Harihara and Bukka
Raya to mark their accession.
(B) It was decorated with delicately carved pillars.
(C) The halls in the temple were used for programmes of music, dance,
drama.
(D) The temple was built over centuries.
 
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (B), (C) and (D) only
options.mistakeAnalysis: Correct answer. Accurately solves the problem for Syllabus Core.

options.text: (A), (B) and (D) only
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Inverts the governing property or boundary condition.

options.text: (A), (B) and (C) only
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Applies an adjacent or reciprocal mathematical relation.

options.text: (A), (B), (C) and (D)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Confuses related NCERT concepts or attributes.

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
For Syllabus Core (History of Buddhism and Jainism (Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings)):
The Virupaksha temple was built over centuries, with inscriptions suggesting earliest shrines dated to the 9th-10th centuries. Krishnadeva Raya substantially expanded the complex: he built the hall in front of the main shrine to mark his accession in 1509 and constructed the eastern gopuram. The halls were decorated with delicately carved pillars and served diverse civic and sacred purposes, such as hosting music, dance, drama, and celebrating divine marriages. Statement (A) is false because Krishnadeva Raya built the hall, making (B), (C), and (D) correct.

Therefore, option (A) is the correct answer.

questionText: The term 'matrilocal' residence means:

options.text:
The practice where men after marriage remain in their natal home and their
wives may come to stay with them.
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Inverts the governing property or boundary condition.

options.text:
The practice where men-women after marriage does not stay with their
families and move to a new home.
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Applies an adjacent or reciprocal mathematical relation.

options.text:
The practice where women after marriage remain in their natal home with
their children and the husbands may come to stay with them.
options.mistakeAnalysis: Correct answer. Accurately solves the problem for Syllabus Core.

options.text:
The practice where women after marriage move to the natal home of their
husbands and their children stays with their parents.
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Confuses related NCERT concepts or attributes.

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
For Syllabus Core (History of Buddhism and Jainism (Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings)):
In anthropological and historical terminology:
- Patrilocal residence is where the wife moves to the husband's home after marriage.
- Matrilocal residence is a practice where women after marriage remain in their natal home with their children and their husbands come to live or stay with them (observed in matrilineal societies such as the Nayars of Kerala and some early communities reflected in Satavahana inscriptions).
- Neolocal residence is where newly-weds move to a completely new home.

Therefore, option (C) is the correct answer.

questionText:
Read the Passage and answer the questions:
 
                                                                                                     Gandhiji on the
Indian Elite
 
When his turn came to speak, Gandhiji charged the Indian elite with a lack
of concern for the labouring poor. The opening of the BHU, he said, was
“certainly a most gorgeous show”. But he worried about the contrast
between the “richly bedecked noblemen” present and “millions of the
poor” Indians who were absent. Gandhiji told the privileged invitees that
“there is no salvation for India unless you strip yourself of this jewellery
and hold it in trust for your countrymen in India”. “There can be no spirit of
self-government about us,” he went on, “if we take away or allow others to
take away from the peasants almost the whole of the results of their labour.
Our salvation can only come through the farmer. Neither the lawyers, nor
the doctors, nor the rich landlords are going to secure it.” The opening of
the BHU was an occasion for celebration, marking as it did the opening of a
nationalist university, sustained by Indian money and Indian initiative. But
rather than adopt a tone of self-congratulation, Gandhiji chose instead to
remind those present of the peasants and workers who constituted a
majority of the Indian population, yet were unrepresented in the audience.
Gandhiji’s speech at Banaras in February 1916 was, at one level, merely a
statement of fact – namely, that Indian nationalism was an elite
phenomenon, a creation of lawyers and doctors and landlords.
At the opening of which institution did Gandhiji made the following
statement, "a most gorgeous show"?
